SEO and AI search · Edtech

Getting DigitalWitch's new website found

Problem

DigitalWitch had a new website and nothing behind it. No blog, no sitemap, and no way to see how it was doing on Google. The only people finding it already knew the name.

What I did

  • First, I looked at what people were actually trying to do. Someone searching "best IT training in Nigeria" wants something different from someone searching "how to work from home", so each got different content.
  • I built a keyword plan of 450+ keywords: 20 priority ones, 125 long-tail ones across 10 topics, and 324+ more for local searches, problem searches, AI questions and content clusters.
  • Each keyword got an intent, a competition level, a priority and a home page on the site.
  • For people ready to pick a course: "best IT training in Nigeria", "online IT support course Nigeria", "learn IT support without experience".
  • For local searches: "IT Training Lagos", "IT Course Abuja", "Online Tech School Nigeria".
  • For people who have never heard of DigitalWitch: "no experience remote jobs", "how to work from home", "jobs that pay in dollars".
  • For people hunting for a job: "entry level tech jobs", "remote customer support jobs", "virtual assistant jobs".
  • For AI tools: questions like "Can I learn tech without a degree?" and "Which tech skill can I learn in 3 months?", each matched to the page that should answer it.
  • I grouped the articles into four clusters and wrote the easy wins first: low competition, high intent.
  • I set up Search Console on 18 July 2026, submitted a 500-page sitemap on 24 July, and tracked the numbers from there.

Result

Search "medical virtual assistant course" on Google in Nigeria and DigitalWitch is in the top 3 results, alongside Udemy (checked 6 November 2026; the exact order varies by device). In the first month alone, people from 39 countries found it through 200+ different searches.

Last 3 months vs the 3 before. CTR fell from 39.4% to 9.2% and average position moved from 2.4 to 7.3. That is normal when a site goes from ranking for a handful of easy terms to ranking for hundreds.

Technical SEO · Edtech

Fixing DigitalWitch's technical SEO

Problem

Search Console was full of errors. Google was even treating the staging copy of the site as a separate website, and it was taking 11 clicks and 273 impressions away from the real one.

What I did

  • I audited the site and gave the developer a dated list of 11 issues.
  • Among them: 87 soft 404s, 30 duplicate pages with no canonical tag, 28 broken pages and 5 server errors.
  • I got SEO fields added to the blog editor: meta title, meta description, slug, author and date.
  • I tested the article schema in Google's Rich Results Test on 2 August 2026.
  • I recorded the mobile PageSpeed score as a baseline.
  • I wrote the FAQPage schema code for the developer.

Result

The developer implemented the fixes. The blog SEO fields and article schema are live and tested.

SEO and technical · Digital health

Getting Medituri found, fast and clean

Problem

The medical content was solid, but almost nobody outside Medituri's own audience could find it. Most searches were for the brand name. Pages were slow, several were fighting over the same keywords, and search engines and AI tools struggled to read them.

What I did

  • I researched keywords and planned content around the gaps.
  • I rewrote titles and meta descriptions in the words people actually type, not textbook language.
  • I wrote posts with question headings, the answer up front and an FAQ at the end, so Google's AI Overviews and ChatGPT can quote them.
  • I set up Cloudflare cache rules to speed up the site and improve Core Web Vitals.
  • I connected Search Console to my AI tools so I can check performance in minutes.

Web design · Performance · Digital health

Redesigning medituri.com and making it fast

Problem

The site looked dated and didn't work well on phones. On mobile, the header buttons ran off the screen. Worse, the contact forms had been failing quietly since at least September 2026, so about 40 enquiries never reached anyone. Mobile PageSpeed was 68, and the main image took 9.3 seconds to load.

What I did

  • I redesigned the homepage, header, footer and blog page in Elementor, starting from mobile, in Medituri's brand colours.
  • I swapped the long hero paragraph for three short, clear promises.
  • I built a partnership page for sponsors, investors and health organisations, with a form that goes straight to the team inbox.
  • I fixed the forms by routing the site's email through Google Workspace.
  • I restyled the blog post headers so the "Written by" and "Reviewed by" bylines stand out.
  • I converted images to WebP, made lighter versions for phones, loaded the hero image first and set up caching.
  • I fixed accessibility issues like colour contrast and heading order.

Result

mobile PageSpeed
before: 68
3.5s
main image load (LCP)
before: 9.3s

before: 89

Enquiries now reach the team, and the site finally works properly on phones.

Getting Medituri read by AI tools

Problem

A lot of people now ask ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity instead of Google, and never click through to a website. You can rank well on Google and still be missing from those answers.

What I did

I restructured Medituri's content so AI tools can read it and quote it. When someone asks about malaria treatment or medication safety in Nigeria, I want Medituri to be one of the sources.

Process

How I work

I don't start with writing. I start with these questions.

  1. Keywords. What are people searching for, and does it matter to the business?
  2. Intent. What does the person searching actually want?
  3. The competition. What do the pages already ranking cover, and what are they missing?
  4. What's already on the site. Sometimes improving an old page beats writing a new one.
  5. The technical side. Can Google crawl and index the page? Is anything holding it back?
  6. The goal. Customers, awareness or enquiries? The answer changes what I write.

Every post should have a reason to exist beyond "we need to publish something".

What goes into every article

SEO

  • The answer to the main question comes in the first 150 words.
  • Every H2 reads like something a real person would search.
  • 10 FAQs per article, using the exact words people type.
  • Article and FAQPage schema on every post.

Internal links

  • I link each article to other articles on the site, so readers and Google can move around.

AEO, answer engine optimization

  • A direct answer of 40 to 60 words comes right after every H2.
  • Technical terms start with a plain definition.
  • How-to posts are numbered steps.
  • People Also Ask questions become H3 headings with direct answers.
  • Comparisons go in tables.

GEO, generative engine optimization

  • Key facts and salary figures go near the top, never buried.
  • I cite verified outside sources inside the text, so AI tools can pick them up.
  • I write in short, clearly labelled chunks that make sense on their own.
  • Each FAQ answer is complete in 2 to 4 sentences.

Content strategy

  • On a new domain I start with very low and low competition keywords.
  • Every article carries Nigeria specific context.
  • I start with the virtual assistant cluster because it has the widest audience, then build outward.
  • Every week I check Search Console: impressions, clicks, CTR and average position.
